scenes.text: One model searches a million documents and answers a yes or no question. How can a single cosine do both?
scenes.say: One model searches a corpus of millions, and answers yes or no questions. How can one cosine do both?

scenes.headline: How MetaEncoder turns a chat model into an encoder
scenes.sub: One tower, the last token, and options as candidates
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Fenna! Meta's MetaEncoder turns a thirty billion parameter chat model into an embedding model. Let's see how, and what it can decide.

scenes.title: Three ways to score
scenes.sub: Read the candidates together, or embed them apart
scenes.say: Chapter one. Three ways to score a candidate.

left.title: Read them together
items: Constrained decoder: letters in one prompt
left.say: A cross-encoder reads the request with each candidate. A constrained decoder lists every option as a letter. Both are accurate, and neither can cache a thing.

right.title: Embed them apart
items: Scales to millions, through one vector
right.say: A bi-encoder embeds the request and each candidate separately and compares them by cosine. Candidates are embedded once, so it scales to millions. MetaEncoder is one of these.

scenes.title: One tower, not two
scenes.sub: A chat model, its output layer removed
scenes.say: Chapter two. One tower, not two.

steps.term: Vision tower: turns pixels into tokens
steps.say: Pictures go through Muse Glimmer's own vision tower. Every twenty-eight by twenty-eight pixels become one token at the decoder's width.
Those tokens sit in one sequence with the text: the task instruction, then the input. The same fifty-two layer decoder reads it all.

steps.term: Last-token pooling: read the final position
steps.say: Nothing is averaged. Under causal attention, only the last token has seen everything, so its hidden state is the embedding.
Version one adds a square head and normalises to unit length. Queries, documents and answer options all come out the same way.
Hand the wrapper a video as a list of frames.
It keeps eight, evenly spaced, first and last included. Each one goes in as its own image. There is no temporal pooling at all.
The decoder reads the frames and the question in order. Training never went past sixteen thousand tokens, and inputs are never truncated.
Out come six thousand six hundred and fifty-six numbers: about twenty-six kilobytes in float thirty-two, for every vector you store.

scenes.credit: Meta's demo gallery, from the v0 model

steps.say: This is what the model sees: eight frames of a test clip. Asked where the dog is sitting, it puts almost all its probability on couch.

scenes.title: A decision is a retrieval
scenes.sub: The options are a very short corpus
scenes.say: Chapter three. A decision is a retrieval.

params.query: Which topic is the query about?
legend: The request and each option, embedded apart
The closest option has the largest cosine
Hotter temperature: flatter bars, same winner

steps.say: Here is a choice question from the model card. The request and each option are embedded separately, by the same network, as unit vectors.

steps.term: Cosine: how closely two directions agree
steps.say: The option pointing most nearly the same way as the request has the largest cosine. That is the answer.
To turn cosines into probabilities, divide by the training temperature, point zero two, and take a softmax. A small cosine gap becomes a confident answer.
Raise the temperature and the bars flatten, but the winner never moves. Calibration changes how sure the model sounds, never what it answers.

parts.say: Training uses the same softmax. Each request is scored against its candidates.

parts.note: only the request picks; candidates never pick back
parts.say: Unlike CLIP, it runs in one direction only. A candidate like No never has to find its question.

parts.note: negatives: the batch, or the row's own options
parts.say: For search, the negatives are everyone else's documents in the batch. For a decision, they are the row's own wrong options. The loss is the evaluation.

scenes.title: Options in the question
scenes.sub: Letting the request see what it competes with
scenes.say: Chapter four. Putting the options in the question.

scenes.title: MMLU, as the prompt changes
scenes.note: MetaEncoder v0, the paper's Tables 3 and 4
scenes.say: A bi-encoder's request never sees the options. So list them in the prompt. On MMLU that lifts accuracy from point five six to point seven five, and letter plus text adds three points.

scenes.title: What the numbers say
scenes.say: Chapter five. What the numbers say.

steps.say: This table on the card is all the evidence for version one. On decisions and multiple choice, it leads most rows.
Retrieval is closer than the post says. A clear win on text search, a whisker on images, a tie on video, and a loss on documents, against a model a third its size.

scenes.title: JevBench hard, items right of 111
scenes.say: And on the hardest decision split, version one went backwards. Eighty-two right became seventy-six, while Open-Jev gets eighty-five.

scenes.title: Where one vector runs out
scenes.sub: Reasoning has to come from somewhere
scenes.say: Chapter six. Where one vector runs out.

steps.say: The paper tests itself against its own base model. Allowed to think before answering, the decoder jumps from about point five to point seven two on MMMU.
Give MetaEncoder that reasoning as context and it climbs from point five seven to point seven one. One forward pass cannot do the thinking itself.

scenes.title: What the release leaves out
scenes.say: Three things to know before you use it.

items.say: The paper describes the earlier checkpoint. Version one's evidence is a single picture.
The evaluation repository's own reference file puts video retrieval four points below the paper.
And version one ships with no licence at all. Version zero is Apache two point oh.

scenes.text: A decision can be a retrieval over a short list: embed the options once, write them into the question, pick by cosine.
scenes.say: A decision can be a retrieval over a short list. Embed the options once, write them into the question, and pick by cosine.

recap: One chat model, last token as embedding
Fast first pass; reasoning goes elsewhere
scenes.say: One chat model, read at its last token. Decisions as a softmax over cosines. A fast first pass, reasoning elsewhere. Thanks for watching!
